definition: The port on which a frame enters a device. Egress is the port on which it leaves; ordinary flooding excludes ingress, while configured hairpin/reflective-relay modes can allow same-port forwarding.
example: A broadcast entering port 3 floods to eligible other ports in its VLAN.

definition: A switch watching multicast group-membership messages so it can send multicast frames only to ports with interested receivers instead of flooding them.
example: With IGMP snooping, an IPTV stream reaches only the set-top boxes that joined it.

definition: A special switch mode that may send a frame back out of the port it arrived on, used for example with virtual machines behind one port. Ordinary bridging never does this.
example: Hairpin mode lets two VMs on one host talk through the external switch.

definition: An attack that sends frames from huge numbers of fake source MAC addresses to fill a switch's MAC table, hoping the switch will then flood unknown-unicast traffic to the attacker.
example: A tool sending 100,000 frames per second with random source MACs can exhaust a small switch's table.

definition: Switch features that limit how many MAC addresses a port may learn and what happens on violation (drop, alert or shut the port). They contain MAC flooding attacks.
example: A correctly enforced source-address learning limit can constrain a flooding attack; violation actions and other security requirements still need configuration.

definition: Forging an identity field, such as a source MAC or IP address, so traffic appears to come from someone else.
example: A MAC flooding tool sends frames with spoofed source addresses.

definition: Virtual LAN: a separate, isolated broadcast domain created in switch configuration, so one physical switch fabric can carry several LANs. Traffic between VLANs must be routed.
example: Staff, guest Wi-Fi and phones can share switches but sit in three VLANs.

definition: The IEEE standard for VLANs and bridging. It defines the 4-byte VLAN tag inserted after the source MAC address, and now also contains the spanning-tree protocols.
example: An 802.1Q-tagged frame carries TPID 0x8100 followed by a 12-bit VLAN ID.

definition: The 4 bytes 802.1Q inserts after the source MAC address: TPID (2 bytes), then PCP, DEI and the VLAN ID (2 bytes). Priority tagging uses VLAN ID 0 to carry only a priority.
example: Adding a VLAN tag to a 1518-byte frame makes it 1522 bytes.

definition: Tag protocol identifier: the first 16 bits of a VLAN tag, sitting where the EtherType would be. 0x8100 marks an 802.1Q tag and 0x88A8 an 802.1ad outer tag.
example: A receiver seeing 0x8100 after the source MAC knows a VLAN tag follows.

definition: Priority code point: the 3-bit priority field in a VLAN tag (values 0–7), used for quality of service.
example: Voice traffic is often marked with PCP 5.

definition: Drop eligible indicator: a 1-bit field in a VLAN tag marking a frame that may be dropped first under congestion.
example: A provider can mark traffic above a customer's contracted rate with DEI = 1.

definition: VLAN identifier: the 12-bit field naming a frame's VLAN. Of its 4096 values, 0 means priority-only and 4095 is reserved, leaving 4094 assignable VLANs (1–4094).
example: A frame tagged with VID 20 belongs to VLAN 20.

definition: Quality of service: treating some traffic preferentially, for example queueing voice ahead of bulk downloads, based on markings such as PCP.
example: QoS can keep a video call smooth while a backup runs.

definition: A switch port configured for an access VLAN, normally carrying untagged host data for that VLAN. Voice VLANs, priority tags and product-specific settings can add exceptions.
example: A normal untagged desk-PC frame is classified into its access VLAN.

definition: A switch port that carries several VLANs, usually distinguishing them with 802.1Q tags, to another switch, a router or a hypervisor.
example: The link between two floor switches is a trunk port carrying all ten VLANs.

definition: The VLAN that untagged frames on a trunk port are assigned to. Depending on configuration it may also be sent tagged, or untagged frames may be refused.
example: A trunk with native VLAN 1 puts any untagged frame it receives into VLAN 1.

definition: A VLAN reserved for IP phones on an otherwise ordinary access port, typically tagged so the phone's traffic is separated and prioritised.
example: A desk phone with a PC behind it uses the voice VLAN while the PC stays untagged.

definition: A switch that can also route IP packets between VLANs in hardware.
example: Inter-VLAN traffic in an office core often goes through a layer 3 switch rather than a separate router.

definition: A switch or access-point setting that stops devices on the same VLAN or Wi-Fi network from talking directly to each other at layer 2.
example: A correctly configured isolation policy can restrict peer-to-peer access; exact scope and exceptions depend on the switch or access point.

definition: Provider bridging ("Q-in-Q"): stacking a second, outer VLAN tag (TPID 0x88A8) in front of a customer's 802.1Q tag so a provider can carry many customers' VLANs.
example: A carrier uses 802.1ad to keep each customer's 4094 VLANs separate inside its own.

definition: The 24-bit identifier in a VXLAN header naming a virtual layer 2 network, allowing about 16 million of them instead of 4094 VLANs.
example: Each tenant in a cloud data centre can get its own VNI.

definition: An Ethernet frame larger than the basic 1500-byte Ethernet payload, often used with an IP MTU near 9000 bytes. The supported size and path constraints depend on equipment; encapsulated or fragmented traffic and path-MTU adaptation require separate accounting.
example: A storage path can use larger packets only where the actual transmitted sizes are supported.

definition: A hardware signal that makes the CPU stop and handle an event, such as a network card receiving packets. Interrupt moderation batches several packets per interrupt.
example: With interrupt moderation, a NIC might raise one interrupt for every 50 received frames.

definition: Work a network card does in hardware on the CPU's behalf, such as computing checksums or splitting large sends into segments.
example: A segmentation-offload send may be divided into several wire-sized segments; the count depends on payload size, headers and negotiated options.

definition: Two devices or links on one path configured with different MTUs, so packets the sender thinks are legal are too big for some hop. Unless fragmentation or path-MTU discovery fixes it, large packets vanish.
example: A jumbo-frame server sending 9000-byte packets across a 1500-byte link hits an MTU mismatch.

definition: Multicast DNS: name lookup on a local network by multicasting queries to 224.0.0.251 (IPv4), used to find printers and other local devices without a DNS server.
example: A Mac looks up "printer.local" with mDNS.

definition: A tool that sends ICMP echo requests and reports whether replies come back and how long they take. It tests reachability and round-trip time.
example: ping -4 -s 1472 -M do sends a 1500-byte IPv4 packet that must not be fragmented.

definition: Maximum segment size: a TCP handshake option advertising a receive limit for TCP data, excluding fixed IP and TCP headers. When deriving an advertised value from an MTU, subtract those fixed headers without additionally subtracting options; the sender reduces actual per-packet payload for IP/TCP options. On-path middleboxes can rewrite the SYN option (“MSS clamping”) for path constraints, while ordinary IP routing does not inherently change this TCP field.
example: On a 1500-byte MTU path with minimal headers the MSS is 1460 bytes.

definition: Network interface card: the hardware that connects a computer to a network, containing the MAC and PHY. NICs compute Ethernet CRCs in hardware.
example: A server NIC may count CRC errors that reveal a bad cable.

definition: A large networking equipment vendor whose switches and routers, and terms such as PortFast, are common in enterprise networks.
example: PortFast is Cisco's name for an STP edge port.

definition: Address Resolution Protocol (RFC 826): resolving a protocol address to a link-layer address, commonly an IPv4 next-hop address to an Ethernet MAC. An initial Ethernet lookup normally broadcasts a request; normal replies are unicast, while other probe and announcement forms differ. ARP itself does not authenticate mappings.
example: Before sending to its gateway 192.168.1.1, a laptop ARPs for the gateway's MAC address.

definition: An IP network defined by a prefix. Hosts normally treat destinations in a configured on-link prefix as directly reachable, but actual connectivity also depends on the link, routes, isolation and neighbour resolution.
example: 192.168.1.20 and 192.168.1.66 are on the same /24 subnet; 8.8.8.8 is not.

definition: The number after the slash in an address like 192.168.1.20/24: how many leading bits form the network prefix. /24 means the first 24 bits (three bytes) are the network, leaving 256 addresses.
Another way of writing the prefix length: a 32-bit value with 1s over the network part, such as 255.255.255.0 for /24. A host uses it to decide whether a destination is on its own subnet.
example: A host wrongly configured with 255.255.0.0 instead of 255.255.255.0 thinks far more addresses are local.

definition: A next-hop router used by a default route when no more specific usable route matches. A destination outside the local subnet can instead match another specific route, so it need not always use the default gateway.
example: A laptop at 192.168.1.20/24 sends traffic for 8.8.8.8 to its default gateway, 192.168.1.1.

definition: The route used when no more specific route matches, pointing at the default gateway. A connected route covers the host's own subnet and is reached directly.
example: With only a connected /24 route and a default route, everything outside the /24 goes to the gateway.

definition: A host's table of recently learned IP-to-MAC mappings, so it need not ARP for every packet. On Linux, ip neigh shows it; on macOS and Windows, arp -a.
example: A gateway entry stays in the ARP cache while traffic keeps confirming it.

definition: Commands that show the neighbour (ARP) cache: ip neigh on Linux and arp -a on macOS and Windows.
example: Running ip neigh on a Linux host lists each neighbour's IP, MAC and state, such as REACHABLE or STALE.

definition: An ARP operation asking for a link-layer mapping. An initial Ethernet/IPv4 lookup is normally broadcast; unicast requests can probe a known neighbour. The target hardware field is unknown for an initial query and is not generally a requirement to contain zeros.
example: "Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.20" is an ARP request.

definition: The answer to an ARP request, normally unicast to the asker: "this IP address is at this MAC address".
example: "192.168.1.1 is at a4:91:b1:..." is an ARP reply.

definition: ARP header fields: HTYPE (hardware type, 1 for Ethernet), PTYPE (protocol type, 0x0800 for IPv4), HLEN and PLEN (address lengths, 6 and 4) and OPER (operation: 1 for request, 2 for reply).
example: An ARP reply has OPER = 2 and the target MAC filled in.

definition: A neighbour-cache entry not recently confirmed. Linux marks entries stale after a randomised "reachable time" (base 30 s, randomised to 15–45 s) but may keep using them while it seeks confirmation.
example: After 45 s without confirmation a Linux ARP entry can show STALE in ip neigh.

definition: An ARP message a host sends unprompted about its own address, to announce or update its IP-to-MAC mapping on the LAN. It is used for failover and also, unfortunately, by spoofing attacks.
example: After a failover, the new server sends gratuitous ARP so neighbours learn its MAC for the shared IP.

definition: An ARP request with sender IP 0.0.0.0 that a host sends before using an address, to check that no other host already has it (RFC 5227).
example: A host that receives a reply to its ARP probe knows the address is taken.

definition: A broadcast ARP request with sender and target IP both set to the host's own address, telling other hosts to refresh their mappings (RFC 5227).
example: A host that has just claimed an address sends ARP announcements.

definition: The RFC 5227 procedure of probing an IPv4 address before using it and watching for others using it, to catch two hosts with the same address.
example: RFC 5227 probing can abandon a candidate address on conflict; an already configured host follows different defend-or-relinquish rules.

definition: An IP address provided through a logical service, rather than necessarily tied permanently to one physical interface. It can move between active/standby devices or be served through other arrangements such as anycast.
example: Two load balancers share the VIP 10.0.0.10; after failover the standby owns it.

definition: Switching service to a standby system when the active one fails.
example: During failover the standby load balancer takes over the virtual IP.

definition: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (RFC 9568): lets several routers share a virtual IP and a virtual MAC so hosts' default gateway keeps working if one router fails.
example: With VRRP’s shared virtual MAC, failover can retain host mappings while forwarding tables learn the new active location; recovery still depends on failure detection and implementation.

definition: A MAC address shared by a group of redundant devices and owned by whichever is active, so neighbours' ARP mappings need not change on failover.
example: VRRP uses virtual MACs of the form 00:00:5e:00:01:xx.

definition: Sending forged ARP messages that map someone else's IP address (often the gateway's) to the attacker's MAC, so their traffic flows through the attacker.
example: An attacker tells a victim "192.168.1.1 is at my MAC" and becomes a man in the middle.

definition: An attack in which the attacker secretly relays traffic between two parties, able to read, alter or drop it. Properly authenticated encryption stops reading and undetected alteration but not dropping.
example: Successful ARP poisoning can redirect the affected next-hop traffic through an attacker; it does not prove that every traffic path is redirected.

definition: An attack that makes a service or network unavailable, for example by dropping or flooding traffic.
example: A man in the middle who simply discards packets causes a denial of service.

definition: Data that describes other data rather than being the data itself. For network traffic it means who talks to whom, when, how much and how often; encryption usually hides content but not all of this metadata.
example: Even with TLS, an observer sees the server's IP address and the sizes and timing of packets.

definition: Secure Shell: an encrypted, authenticated protocol for remote login and command execution.
example: An SSH connection with correctly verified server identity protects encrypted contents against an ARP-based intermediary, though that intermediary can still drop traffic.

definition: A switch feature that checks ARP messages on untrusted ports against trusted IP-to-MAC bindings (usually from DHCP snooping) and drops forged ones.
example: With DAI enabled, a guest PC claiming to be the gateway in ARP has its messages dropped.

definition: Access control list: an ordered list of permit and deny rules. ARP ACLs give Dynamic ARP Inspection the valid mappings for hosts with static addresses.
example: An ARP ACL might permit only 10.0.0.5 at 00:11:22:33:44:55 on a server port.

definition: A switch feature that watches DHCP traffic, blocks DHCP servers on untrusted ports and records which IP was leased to which MAC on which port. Those bindings feed Dynamic ARP Inspection.
example: DHCP snooping records that 192.168.1.20 was leased to 3c:22:fb:11:22:33 on port 7.

definition: A port configured to bypass a particular inspection check. DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection have distinct trust configuration; being trusted for one does not universally make a port trusted for every security feature.
example: An administrator must configure and review the trust boundary for the specific inspection feature.

definition: A manually configured IP-to-MAC mapping that ARP replies cannot overwrite. It protects that one mapping but is tedious to maintain.
example: A server might pin its gateway with a static ARP entry.

definition: A monitoring tool that records IP-to-MAC pairings seen on a LAN and alerts when one changes, which can reveal ARP spoofing.
example: arpwatch emails an alert when the gateway's IP suddenly maps to a new MAC.

definition: IPv6's replacement for ARP and more (RFC 4861): ICMPv6 messages for finding neighbours' link-layer addresses, routers and prefixes. Like ARP it is unauthenticated by default.
example: An IPv6 host sends a neighbour solicitation where an IPv4 host would send an ARP request.

definition: The IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages that play ARP's roles: a solicitation asks for a neighbour's link-layer address, and an advertisement answers or announces it.
example: A forged neighbour advertisement can redirect IPv6 traffic just as forged ARP does for IPv4.

definition: An IPv6 multicast address formed from a unicast or anycast address’s low 24 bits and the solicited-node prefix. Initial address resolution uses neighbour solicitation to that group; reachability probes can instead be unicast.
example: For an address ending 0d:ab:cd the solicited-node address is ff02::1:ff0d:abcd.

definition: Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971): an extension using cryptographic mechanisms, including signed messages and address-related checks, to protect Neighbor Discovery. Deployment and support must be checked for the actual systems.
example: SEND protection requires compatible hosts and appropriate configuration; signing alone is not an assumed default.

definition: A switch feature that blocks IPv6 router advertisements arriving on host ports, stopping rogue devices from posing as routers. It does not stop forged neighbour advertisements.
example: With RA Guard, a laptop cannot announce itself as the network's IPv6 router.

definition: An IPv6 Neighbor Discovery message in which a router announces itself and the prefixes hosts should use.
example: IPv6 hosts learn their default router from router advertisements.

definition: Validating IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages against learned or configured bindings to restrict spoofed address claims. Feature names and supported checks depend on the product; some Cisco releases replace the older ND-inspection feature with SISF-based device tracking.
example: ND inspection drops a neighbour advertisement claiming an address bound to another port.

definition: A flood of broadcast frames, typically from a switching loop with no spanning tree, that multiply and circulate until they consume the network's capacity.
example: A patch cable looped between two wall ports can cause a broadcast storm that takes an office offline.

definition: A cycle in the active layer-2 forwarding topology. Basic Ethernet provides no forwarding hop-count expiry, so a circulating broadcast can persist until congestion, filtering, faults or a loop-prevention mechanism removes it.
example: A triangle with all relevant ports forwarding can form a loop; physical redundancy with a blocked port need not.

definition: A switch repeatedly relearning the same MAC address on different ports, a classic symptom of a switching loop.
example: During a loop the switch logs host A moving between ports 1 and 2 many times a second.

definition: A short cable with connectors at both ends, used to connect devices to wall sockets or patch panels.
example: Joining two forwarding ports in the same layer-2 domain can create a loop unless the topology or protective features prevent it.

definition: Spanning Tree Protocol: lets bridges agree on a loop-free tree across a physically redundant network and block the remaining ports, unblocking one if an active link fails. Originally IEEE 802.1D.
example: In a triangle of switches, STP blocks one port so broadcasts cannot circulate.

definition: Bridge protocol data unit: the spanning-tree message switches exchange (every 2 seconds by default), saying in effect "I think the root is X and my cost to it is C".
example: A port that stops receiving BPDUs from its root path will eventually recompute the tree.

definition: The spanning-tree hello timer, commonly two seconds by default. In classic STP non-root bridges relay root information; RSTP bridges originate periodic BPDUs themselves.
example: Do not infer a universal “ten missed packets” failure rule from hello and max-age defaults; message age and protocol version matter.

definition: The reserved multicast MAC address 01:80:c2:00:00:00 to which spanning-tree BPDUs are sent. Bridges process frames to it rather than forwarding them.
example: A packet capture of STP shows BPDUs sent to 01:80:c2:00:00:00.

definition: The elected reference bridge in a spanning-tree instance, chosen by the lowest bridge ID. Other bridges select their best paths towards it; the root need not be physically central or lie on every data path.
example: A priority of 4096 beats 32768 for the same applicable instance, but another lower bridge ID can still win.

definition: A switch's spanning-tree identity: a priority field (with an extended system ID) followed by its MAC address. Lower wins; priority is compared first.
example: Bridge ID 4096/f8:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff beats 32768/00:00:0c:00:00:00 because 4096 < 32768.

definition: The configurable, most significant part of a bridge ID, set in steps of 4096 (default commonly 32768). Lowering it makes a switch more likely to become root.
example: Give the intended root priority 4096 and its backup 8192.

definition: The low 12 bits of the bridge priority field, holding a spanning-tree instance number (the VLAN number in per-VLAN STP), which is why priorities move in steps of 4096.
example: In per-VLAN STP, the bridge for VLAN 10 at priority 32768 advertises 32778.

definition: Running a separate spanning tree for each VLAN, a Cisco approach, so different VLANs can block different links.
example: With per-VLAN STP, VLAN 10 can use link A while VLAN 20 uses link B.

definition: The selected best port towards the root on a non-root bridge, based on received root information, path cost and tie-breakers. Its role does not guarantee it is already in the forwarding state during convergence.
example: S2's root port faces S3 because 4 + 4 = 8 is cheaper than its direct cost of 19.

definition: The sum of per-link costs along a path to a destination; lower is preferred. In spanning tree it is the cost from a switch to the root bridge, and in the short cost table 100 Mbit/s costs 19, 1 Gbit/s 4 and 10 Gbit/s 2. Routing protocols such as OSPF use their own link costs.
example: Two gigabit hops to the root cost 4 + 4 = 8, cheaper than one 100 Mbit/s hop at 19.

definition: The port selected to advertise the best spanning-tree information for a segment, using root identity, path cost and tie-breakers. On the simple point-to-point examples, the root-facing sender is designated; role and current forwarding state remain distinct.
example: On the S2–S3 link, S3's end is designated because its cost to root (4) beats S2's (8).

definition: A classic-STP port in the blocking state receives relevant BPDUs but does not forward user data or learn source addresses. In a stable simple topology this includes redundant enabled ports outside the root/designated forwarding set; role and state are distinct during convergence.
example: If the active path fails, the blocked port can become the new root port.

definition: Classic STP's intermediate port states: listening (15 s) to make sure the topology has settled, then learning (15 s) to fill the MAC table, before forwarding.
example: With classic default timers and no edge/PortFast shortcut, a transitioning port spends 15 seconds listening and 15 learning.

definition: The STP timer (15 seconds by default) a port spends in each of the listening and learning states.
example: Two forward delays of 15 s give the classic 30-second wait after link-up.

definition: The STP timer (20 seconds by default) for how long a switch keeps BPDU information without hearing it refreshed before assuming the path has failed.
example: The familiar 50-second example combines a 20-second ageing wait with two 15-second forwarding delays; it is not a bound for every failure or configuration.

definition: Settling on consistent layer-2 forwarding after a topology change. Classic STP with default timers can require transitions around 30–50 seconds; suitable RSTP transitions can be faster, but detection, topology and interoperability determine recovery.
example: An unaffected forwarding path can continue while another part of the topology converges.

definition: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (originally IEEE 802.1w): keeps STP's root election and costs but adds a proposal/agreement handshake and pre-computed alternate ports, so transitions can take under a second.
example: Proposal/agreement and a usable alternate path can speed a transition; a universal one-second recovery time is not guaranteed.

definition: RSTP's handshake on point-to-point links: a switch proposes to make its port forwarding and the neighbour agrees after syncing, skipping the forward-delay timers.
example: Proposal/agreement lets two RSTP switches bring a new link into forwarding almost immediately.

definition: An RSTP port receiving superior information from another bridge and providing an alternate root path while discarding data. It can replace a failed root port when protocol and failure-detection conditions permit; a backup port is a distinct role for the same segment.
example: S3's blocked port in the triangle is an alternate port.

definition: Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol (originally IEEE 802.1s): runs several spanning-tree instances, each serving a group of VLANs, so different VLANs can use different links.
example: With MSTP, odd VLANs can block one uplink and even VLANs the other.

definition: A switch port connected to an end host rather than another switch, so it goes straight to forwarding without the STP delay. Cisco calls this PortFast.
example: Configuring desk ports as edge ports stops laptops waiting 30 s for the network after plugging in.

definition: A feature that disables or otherwise protects a configured port when a BPDU arrives, with behaviour depending on the product and setting. It enforces a host-port assumption when BPDUs are seen; a BPDU does not prove a particular physical device, nor does the guard detect every silent loop.
example: A switch that sends BPDUs into a protected edge port can trigger its configured shutdown.

definition: A protection that stops a port from accepting a better root bridge, so a misconfigured or malicious switch cannot take over as root.
example: Root guard on access-layer ports keeps the core switch as root even if a rogue switch advertises priority 0.

definition: Protections against a link that carries traffic in only one direction: loop guard stops a port forwarding just because BPDUs stopped arriving, and UDLD detects one-way links directly.
example: A fibre pair with one broken strand can create a one-way link that loop guard contains.

definition: Combining eligible parallel links into one logical aggregate. Common flow-hash distribution keeps one flow on one member, while aggregate utilisation and alternative distribution modes depend on implementation and workload.
example: Four 10 Gbit/s members offer 40 Gbit/s nominal aggregate capacity; a single flow commonly remains bounded by one member.

definition: Link Aggregation Control Protocol: the protocol two devices use to agree which links form an aggregate and to detect failed members.
example: LACP drops a member from the bundle when its far end stops responding.

definition: Multi-chassis link aggregation: one link aggregate whose members land on two different switches, giving redundancy without STP blocking. Implementations are vendor-specific.
example: A server dual-homed to two top-of-rack switches with MLAG keeps working if either switch fails.

definition: A data-centre design in which every access (leaf) switch connects to every core (spine) switch, usually with routing between them so all paths can be used.
example: In the simple single-tier fabric, a server-to-server path between different leaves traverses leaf, spine and leaf: three switches.

definition: Equal-cost multipath: a router spreading flows across several equally good next hops, typically by hashing each flow onto one path.
example: With 4 spines, ECMP spreads a leaf's flows over four uplinks.

definition: Adding redundant bits computed from the data so the receiver can tell that something changed on the way. Parity, checksums and CRCs detect errors but cannot fix them.
example: Ethernet detects damaged frames with its CRC-32 and simply drops them.

definition: Forward error correction: sending enough extra redundant bits that the receiver can repair some errors itself, with no retransmission round trip. It costs bandwidth and coding work.
example: High-speed Ethernet PHYs use Reed–Solomon FEC to fix bit errors before the FCS check.

definition: Automatic repeat request: recovering from loss or damage by detecting it (via missing acknowledgements or failed checks) and sending the data again. Stop-and-wait, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat are ARQ schemes.
example: TCP's retransmission of unacknowledged data is a form of ARQ.

definition: The number of bit positions in which two bit strings differ. A code's minimum Hamming distance d between valid codewords lets it detect up to d − 1 flipped bits or correct up to ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋.
example: 1011 and 1001 have a Hamming distance of 1; a single parity bit gives distance 2.

definition: A classic error-correcting code that sends 4 data bits as 7 bits with minimum distance 3, so it corrects any single-bit error.
example: Flip any one of the 7 bits and the decoder finds and fixes it.

definition: One extra bit that makes the count of 1s even (even parity) or odd. It detects any odd number of flipped bits but misses every even number.
example: With even parity, 1011001 gets a parity bit of 0 because it already has four 1s.

definition: A run of damage measured from the first changed bit to the last; the bits in between need not all change. Noise spikes tend to cause bursts rather than isolated flips.
example: Flips at positions 10 and 14 form a burst of length 5.

definition: The 16-bit checksum used by IPv4, UDP and TCP (RFC 1071): add the data as 16-bit words, fold any carry back into the bottom, and invert. Fast in software, but blind to reordered words.
example: Swapping two 16-bit words leaves the Internet checksum unchanged.

definition: A binary arithmetic in which a carry out of the top bit is added back in at the bottom (end-around carry), and negation means inverting every bit.
example: In 16-bit one's complement, 0xFFFF + 0x0001 gives 0x0001 after the carry is wrapped round.

definition: Describes an operation whose result does not depend on the order of its inputs, like addition (a + b = b + a). It is why a plain sum cannot detect reordered data.
The ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) special interest group on data communication, and its leading annual networking research conference.
example: Stone and Partridge's study of checksum failures appeared at SIGCOMM 2000.

definition: A sum of powers of a variable, each with a coefficient, such as x³ + x + 1. A CRC treats a bit string as a polynomial whose coefficients are its bits.
example: The bit string 1011 is the polynomial x³ + x + 1.

definition: The field containing exactly zero and one. Addition and subtraction are XOR and multiplication follows binary one-bit multiplication; CRC polynomial division uses coefficients in this specific field, not an arbitrary finite field.
Exclusive or: a bitwise operation giving 1 when exactly one of its two inputs is 1. It is addition without carries, the core step of CRC division.
The fixed polynomial a CRC divides by, agreed by sender and receiver. Its degree r is the number of check bits, and its choice decides which error patterns are guaranteed to be caught.
example: Ethernet's generator is 0x04C11DB7 with an implicit x³² term.

definition: A chain of one-bit storage cells that move their contents along one place per clock tick. With XOR feedback taps it computes a CRC one bit per tick, cheaply in hardware.
example: A 32-cell shift register with XOR taps computes CRC-32 as bits stream past.

definition: Reversing the order of bits, as real CRC-32 does to its input bytes and result because Ethernet sends each byte least significant bit first.
example: 0xEDB88320 is 0x04C11DB7 bit-reversed.

definition: The CRC of the ASCII string "123456789", published so implementations can verify they compute a CRC variant correctly.
example: CRC-32's check value is 0xCBF43926.

definition: A different 32-bit CRC (the Castagnoli polynomial) used by iSCSI, SCTP and some storage systems, with different error-detection guarantees from Ethernet's CRC-32. Some CPUs accelerate it in hardware.
example: x86 processors with SSE4.2 have an instruction for CRC-32C, not Ethernet's CRC-32.

definition: A widely used compression library; Python's zlib module also provides the standard CRC-32 function.
example: zlib.crc32(b"123456789") returns 0xCBF43926.

definition: Philip Koopman's published tables of CRC polynomials, listing the data lengths up to which each guarantees a given Hamming distance.
example: Koopman's table shows Ethernet's CRC-32 keeps distance 4 up to 91,607 data bits.

definition: A keyed integrity tag designed to make unauthorised message forgery infeasible under its security assumptions. A finite tag does not make successful forgery mathematically impossible; HMAC and AEAD authentication tags provide different constructions.
example: A modified authenticated record is rejected except with the construction’s bounded forgery probability, assuming correct keys and implementation.

definition: Wired Equivalent Privacy: the original, badly broken Wi-Fi security scheme. Its integrity check was a CRC-32, which attackers could recompute after changing data.
example: WEP was replaced by WPA and WPA2 in the 2000s.

definition: A powerful error-correcting code that works on multi-bit symbols, good at fixing bursts. High-speed Ethernet PHYs, CDs and QR codes use it.
example: 100 Gbit/s Ethernet over some optics uses Reed–Solomon FEC.

definition: The simplest ARQ: send one frame, wait for its acknowledgement, then send the next, resending on timeout. On long fast paths the sender is idle almost all the time.
example: With the stated 1500-byte frames, 1 Gbit/s link and 30 ms propagation round trip, stop-and-wait utilisation is about 0.04%, ignoring ACK time and other overhead.

definition: A number in each frame or segment that lets the receiver put data in order and recognise duplicates. With k bits there are 2ᵏ values, after which numbering wraps round to 0.
example: The textbook alternating-bit stop-and-wait model uses a one-bit sequence number, with suitable ordering and packet-lifetime assumptions; arbitrary old duplicates cannot be handled by finite numbering alone.

definition: The time a sender waits for an acknowledgement before assuming loss and retransmitting.
example: If no ACK arrives within the timeout, the stop-and-wait sender resends the frame.

definition: A textbook ARQ model accepting frames only in order with cumulative acknowledgements. On timeout it resends outstanding frames from the oldest unacknowledged one; the usual window bound is one less than the sequence-space size under ordered-channel and bounded-old-duplicate assumptions.
example: If frame 2 of 0–5 is lost, Go-Back-N resends 2, 3, 4 and 5.

definition: A textbook ARQ model that buffers valid in-window out-of-order frames and acknowledges them individually. Unacknowledged frames may be retried on timeout, including after a lost ACK; equal sender and receiver windows use at most half the sequence space under the stated lifetime/channel assumptions.
example: When only frame 2 is lost and all other ACKs arrive, the sender need resend only frame 2.

definition: An acknowledgement meaning "everything up to here has arrived". TCP's ACKs are cumulative byte counts.
example: In the convention where an ACK names the last frame received in order, ACK 5 in Go-Back-N confirms frames 0 to 5 at once.

definition: Frames that have been sent but not yet acknowledged. The window limits how many may be outstanding at once.
example: In the loss-free 1 Gbit/s model with 1500-byte frames and 30 ms propagation round trip, a 2501-frame window covers the full frame-plus-feedback cycle.

definition: A TCP option reporting additional received byte ranges beyond the cumulative ACK. It helps a sender choose loss recovery but does not guarantee that only genuinely missing data is retransmitted; ACK loss, reordering and recovery rules still matter.
example: With SACK, a receiver missing bytes 1000–1999 can say it already has 2000–9999.

definition: Arithmetic that wraps round after reaching a fixed number: "modulo 8" counts 0, 1, …, 7, 0, 1, …. Sequence numbers wrap modulo 2ᵏ, and "a mod b" is the remainder of a divided by b.
example: With 3-bit sequence numbers, the number after 7 is 0.

definition: Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (RFC 7323): using TCP timestamps to reject old segments whose sequence numbers have wrapped round and look new again.
example: On a 10 Gbit/s connection the 32-bit sequence space wraps in under 4 seconds, so PAWS matters.

definition: A ten-byte TCP option carrying a sender timestamp and an echoed timestamp, used for RTT measurement and PAWS. Common alignment uses twelve option-space bytes including padding; payload impact depends on the full header layout.
example: In the stated minimal IPv4 example with twelve timestamp-option/padding bytes, a 1500-byte IP packet leaves 1448 TCP payload bytes.

definition: The probability distribution of how many independent tries it takes to get the first success. If each try fails with probability p, the expected number of tries is 1/(1 − p).
example: With a 50% failure rate you need 2 tries on average.

definition: The long-run average of a random quantity over many repetitions.
example: The expected number of attempts at 1.19% failure is about 1.012.

definition: The fraction of bits received wrongly. With independent bit errors at rate b, an n-bit frame is damaged with probability 1 − (1 − b)ⁿ.
example: At a BER of 10⁻⁶, about 1.2% of 12,000-bit frames have an error.

definition: A position-sensitive checksum maintaining two running sums. It detects many reorderings missed by a plain sum, but modulo arithmetic leaves undetectable patterns, so not every swap is guaranteed to change it.
example: In Fletcher-16, swapping byte values 0 and 255 can leave both modulo-255 sums unchanged.

definition: A cryptographic hash function producing a 256-bit digest. It is designed to make collision and preimage attacks infeasible, rather than guaranteeing a different digest for every changed input; an expected digest needs authentication when an attacker can replace it.
example: Compare a trusted source digest with a digest after destination storage to check across that boundary.

definition: Operating system: the software, such as Linux, Windows or macOS, that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs, including its network stack.
example: Whether a phone uses a private Wi-Fi address depends on its OS version and settings.

definition: Receiving frames or packets in a different sequence from the one sent. The textbook Go-Back-N receiver discards later frames after a gap, while Selective Repeat buffers in-window frames; TCP generally supports out-of-order buffering subject to resources and implementation.
example: If frame 2 is lost, frames 3, 4 and 5 arrive out of order.

definition: Costs paid once for every packet whatever its size: header bytes, table lookups, interrupts and checks. Small packets make it dominate, which is why devices are rated in packets per second as well as bits per second.
example: A router doing a fixed lookup per packet handles 64-byte frames far less efficiently than 1500-byte ones.

definition: The fraction of a link's busy time that carries useful data rather than headers, trailers, preamble, gaps or retransmissions. Multiply it by the link rate to get the useful data rate.
example: A full-size TCP segment on Ethernet is about 94.9% efficient: 1460 data bytes in 1538 byte-times.

definition: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a US university whose OpenCourseWare materials explain channel coding and ARQ protocols, including Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat.
example: MIT OpenCourseWare publishes course notes on ARQ protocols free online.

definition: Version 1.2 of Transport Layer Security (RFC 5246), the predecessor of TLS 1.3. A conventional full TLS 1.2 handshake takes two round trips before application data can flow.
example: A fresh HTTPS connection using TCP and TLS 1.2 spends three round trips (one TCP, two TLS) before the request is sent.

definition: A function mapping data to a fixed-size digest, designed to resist finding collisions, preimages and second preimages. Collisions exist in principle, and an unkeyed digest by itself does not authenticate data if an attacker can replace both data and digest.
example: A trusted SHA-256 reference can detect altered download data with high confidence; it does not locate the damage.

definition: The interface through which a frame or packet leaves a device. Egress tagging policy determines whether a VLAN tag is present on the transmitted frame; ingress is the interface through which it entered.

An RSTP port providing a redundant connection to a segment for which the same bridge already has a designated port. It receives superior information from that same bridge; unlike an alternate root path, it does not necessarily provide another route to the root.

A received Ethernet frame whose frame check sequence does not match the computed value. Standard counters distinguish FCS errors in octet-aligned frames from alignment errors; device-specific counters and causes need their own documentation.
The Ethernet family operating at a 100 Mbit/s MAC data rate. It includes copper and fibre PHYs such as 100BASE-TX and 100BASE-FX, with different media and signalling.

A simplified channel model in which each bit has the same chance of flipping, independently of the other bits. Longer frames then have more opportunities to contain an error; burst errors and residual errors after coding may behave differently.

Choosing the valid codeword with the fewest differing bit positions from a received word. Recovery is guaranteed only while errors leave the original uniquely nearest; heavier damage can lead to an incorrect choice.
